implementation_notes: ASP.NET Core is the dominant realization: an authorization policy is a named set of requirements (IAuthorizationRequirement) evaluated by handlers (AuthorizationHandler<TRequirement>), registered with AddAuthorizationBuilder().AddPolicy and applied declaratively with [Authorize(Policy = ...)] or RequireAuthorization(); the framework's authorization middleware is the Guard and the registered policy with its handlers is the Policy. For resource-based decisions, IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(user, resource, policy) is the direct Policy+Guard equivalent inside application code, returning an AuthorizationResult the caller must honour. What replaces the classic structure: the framework owns the enforcement point and the policy container, so you implement requirements, handlers and registration only; hand-roll a policy object outside ASP.NET Core hosts (workers, console tools) or when the decision must consult a non-HTTP, non-DI service.
idiom_name: ASP.NET Core policy-based authorization (requirements + handlers + authorization middleware)
pitfalls: A policy whose requirement has no registered handler fails every request, and a handler that calls Succeed unconditionally allows every request; both mistakes look like configuration, not code.
UseAuthentication must run before UseAuthorization and both must run after UseRouting; a misplaced middleware leaves endpoints unguarded or always rejected.

Handlers registered with singleton lifetime must not inject scoped services, and resource-based checks must pass the same resource instance that is later mutated - re-querying between check and use reopens the TOCTOU gap.
